section_summary: This section traces the Japanese Army’s growing influence over censorship, personnel policy, military budgets, national mobilization, air defense, and schemes for a totalitarian “national defense state” during 1936–1937. It includes embassy reporting, State Department summaries, filing notes, statutory translations, and newspaper enclosures concerning the February 26 Incident, military propaganda, Soviet and Chinese armaments, and preparations for aerial warfare. The final documents describe large-scale troop embarkations through Kobe after the outbreak of fighting in China and the restrained but apprehensive reaction of Japanese commercial and civilian society.

subfiles.title: Public Resistance to Government Control Bills and the Seditious Literature Emergency Control Law
subfiles.doc_type: despatch conclusion with newspaper clipping enclosure
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Concludes an assessment of public resistance to restrictive legislation and encloses a press version of the proposed law against anonymous seditious publications.
subfiles.summary: Grew says resistance to the Mobilization Secrets Bill shows limits to public docility after February 26; a Japan Advertiser clipping gives provisions of the Seditious Literature Emergency Control Law.

subfiles.title: File Note on Army and Navy Department Appointment Regulations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Cross-references a despatch on regulations restricting senior Army and Navy ministerial appointments to active-list generals and admirals.
subfiles.summary: File note on despatch no. 1864: amendments on Army and Navy Department organization and eligibility of ministers and vice ministers.

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Investigations and Discipline after the February 26 Incident
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reports Army efforts to identify direct-action advocates and restore discipline after the February 26 uprising.
subfiles.summary: After February 26 the Army removed direct-action officers while moderates consolidated control; Terauchi urged discipline and armaments, Kashii was relieved, and the press urged larger forces in Manchukuo and North China.

subfiles.title: Norman H. Davis Conversation with Yoshida on Japanese Expansion
subfiles.from: Norman H. Davis
subfiles.about: Records Yoshida’s assessment that the Japanese Army was reconsidering the consequences of its conquest and expansion program.
subfiles.summary: Note on Norman Davis's talk with Yoshida: the Army believed conquest answered public demands, but wiser elements gaining control now ask diplomats for help.

subfiles.title: Departmental Memorandum on the Seditious Literature Bill
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the purpose of Tokyo telegram no. 1912 and the post-February effort to tighten control over publications and public thought.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: the Seditious Literature law strengthens government control of information and opinion, reflecting official anxiety after the February 26 Incident.

subfiles.title: Temporary Law for the Control of Seditious Documents
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and explains the official translation of Japan’s new law suppressing anonymous or improperly registered seditious publications.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes ministerial instructions urging cautious but vigorous enforcement against clandestine publications and the persons actually responsible rather than nominal editors. He also notes official fears of political meetings, labor disputes, reform societies, spies, and communists after the lifting of martial law. The enclosure translates Law No. 45, prescribing imprisonment, seizure of publications and printing blocks, punishment of attempts, and fines for prohibited distribution.

subfiles.title: Army Affairs, Air Ministry Plans, and the February 26 Trials
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reviews proposals for an Air Ministry, an ex-service graduate organization, the February 26 trials, and the first seizure under the new seditious-literature law.
subfiles.summary: The Army backs an Air Ministry and plans to organize a million former cadets as intermediaries with the public; the War Office briefs on the February 26 trials and martial law, and the first pamphlet is confiscated under new censorship.

subfiles.title: Annual Air Defense Maneuvers
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the fourth annual air-defense exercises in Tokyo, Yokohama, and Kanagawa and related plans to redesign the capital.
subfiles.summary: Civilian patriotic organizations, police, searchlights, antiaircraft units, and defending aircraft practiced firefighting, rescue, gas protection, first aid, and blackout control against simulated attacks from the west and the Pacific. Although officials praised the increasingly effective blackout, they criticized public apathy and recognized that existing defenses could not withstand a mass raid. The Home Ministry consequently advocated wide wooded avenues, underground utilities, reservoirs, fireproof construction, decentralization, and municipal air-defense legislation.

subfiles.title: Departmental Memorandum on Japanese Army Shifts and Promotions
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes personnel changes intended to restore Army discipline after the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: about three thousand Army changes removed officers sympathetic to the insurgents, elevating Sugiyama and Isogai, strengthening War Office ties with the North China Garrison.

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Shifts and Promotions, August 1, 1936
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the disciplinary and political significance of extensive Japanese Army personnel changes.
subfiles.summary: August 1, 1936 Army list quietly moved officers suspected of sympathizing with the February revolt, concentrated personnel authority in the War Minister, and put Sugiyama and Isogai in key posts.

subfiles.title: Japanese Military Conference at Shanghai
subfiles.from: Johnson, United States mission in China
subfiles.about: Reports a July 11–12 conference of Japanese military representatives in Shanghai concerning Sino-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded excerpt indicates that senior Japanese military figures, officers stationed in several parts of China, and reportedly the Japanese ambassador attended the meeting. Subsequent statements suggested differences among the participants and argued that relations could not improve without eliminating anti-Japanese sentiment and strengthening the Hebei–Chahar Political Council.

subfiles.title: Developments in the Japanese Army during July 1936
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews executions and sentences arising from the February 26 Incident, the lifting of martial law, and new defense programs.
subfiles.summary: July 1936: Aizawa executed, sentences for February 26 participants including fifteen executions, martial law lifted, an Air Force Headquarters created, and a six-year defense program demanded.

subfiles.title: Mobilization Plan Advanced by the Army
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes an Army proposal for comprehensive peacetime and wartime mobilization of Japan’s resources and population.
subfiles.summary: Dickover describes the Army's mobilization plan covering raw materials, labor, finance, aviation, food and ideology, seeking complete control of national material and manpower.

subfiles.title: Departmental Memorandum on the Army Pamphlet of November 5
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes the political and foreign-policy themes of the Japanese Army’s November 5 propaganda pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on the Army's November 5 pamphlet: it builds support for budget demands by endorsing a totalitarian state and Manchukuo, claiming Japan stabilizes the Far East; public reaction was indifferent.

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Pamphlet of November 5, 1936
subfiles.doc_type: diplomatic despatch with newspaper clipping enclosures
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes and reproduces press summaries of an Army pamphlet advocating armament expansion, continental military strength, and totalitarian administrative reform.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reports that the pamphlet justified a ten-year or longer rearmament program, claimed priority for defense spending, portrayed the Soviet Union and China as principal threats, and endorsed a constitutionally achieved totalitarian national-defense state. The newspaper enclosures review Soviet and Chinese forces, earlier Japanese reductions, the costs of rearmament, expansion of the Manchurian garrison and air force, and the relationship between industrial mobilization and military power. They argue that Japan must approach parity with Soviet Far Eastern forces while denying that this necessarily entails an unlimited arms race or military dictatorship.

subfiles.title: The Army, the Diet, and the 1937–1938 Budget
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Examines the Army’s position on Diet reform, the Cabinet, military appropriations, and taxation.
subfiles.summary: War Minister Terauchi denied that a radical Diet-reform proposal originated in the War Office but warned against interpreting Japan’s constitutional system through imported democratic ideas. Army leaders pressed the Cabinet for administrative reform and defended their large budget demands while disclaiming responsibility for the resulting taxation and its economic effects.

subfiles.title: The Army’s Position in Japanese Political Affairs
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Assesses the Army’s continuing political predominance after its confrontation with the parties and the fall of the Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: January setbacks did not reduce Army influence; Hayashi's selection is an Army victory and an attempt to control the military; Terauchi says party views are incompatible, and Nagano's mediation failed.

subfiles.title: Supplementary Report on Military and Political Matters in Kobe
subfiles.from: Winthrop R. Scott, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reports the completion of troop embarkations from Kobe and conditions among the city’s Chinese residents.
subfiles.summary: Scott estimates forty small steamers moved troops from Kobe over several days; the Chinese consul general denied Nanjing ordered evacuation, and send-offs showed little war fever.

subfiles.title: Departmental Memorandum on Public Reaction in Kobe
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Kobe consular report on commercial opinion and attitudes toward foreigners during the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Kobe business opinion is loyal but unenthusiastic and worried about costs; friendliness toward the U.S. continues, with less warmth to Britons.

subfiles.title: Military and Political Matters in Kobe
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with enclosed confidential letter
subfiles.from: Winthrop R. Scott, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; enclosure addressed to Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Describes troop embarkations through Kobe and local reactions to the expanding war in China.
subfiles.summary: Scott estimates that between twenty and thirty thousand infantry and cavalry troops left Kobe between August 8 and 10, some apparently traveling through Busan, Seoul, and Dandong, while naval vessels assisted and photography was restricted. Commercial circles displayed loyalty but feared the consequences for an already strained economy, and the wider population showed restrained rather than exuberant patriotism. Attitudes toward Americans remained friendly, feeling toward British nationals was less favorable, Soviet nationals were viewed suspiciously, and Chinese residents had not yet suffered systematic mistreatment.
